b: LeVar Burton is the iconic actor behind roles like Kunta Kinte in Roots and Geordi LaForge in Star Trek: The Next Generation. He was also the host of Reading Rainbow. Below is an excerpt from his memoir, Take My Word for It, out now from Random House.

If you take Roots, Reading Rainbow, Star Trek, all those pieces together, what you get is my Work. But I’m not necessarily talking about the specifics of the characters I played, although I’m sure that’s part of it. I’m talking about the aggregate of it all—what those roles represent in the grand scheme of life.

It is now my understanding that show business has only been my entry point into a broader work. Reading Rainbow gave me the credibility to champion the cause of literacy worldwide and to speak out against the scourge of book bans. It created a legacy that will likely outlive me; at least I hope so. Roots provided me with a platform to discuss racism in America and how Black people have constantly had to navigate life with a hypervigilance that affects every aspect of our lives, health, and communities. Star Trek gave me the authority to address the future of humanity and emphasize how we heal ourselves from the illusion that race, color, creed, and national boundaries are legitimate reasons for conflict. Speaking about my rage à la James Baldwin in the miniseries Clipped opened the door for me to discuss that which lies beneath the surface of most Black people in America. All of this is part of the Work I believe I’ve been sent here to do. The roles were simply vehicles; they are the mechanisms through which the Work is revealed. In short, it’s why I’m here on this planet—what my soul agreed to do when I took this body.

And as I look at my personal evolution alongside my career trajectory, one thing stands out: from Kunta to the Reading Rainbow guy to Geordi, I’ve been blessed to represent a continuum of the Black experience in America, moving from our enslavement, through the present, and on to a star-faring future. For some, that might feel like a heavy thing to carry. But the wild thing is, to me it doesn’t feel like a weight at all. It feels like a privilege. Because, really, who gets to do that? To have grown up in a country where three generations ago it would’ve been illegal for me to know how to read and now be a symbol of literacy? Come on! This lifetime was planned.
